I still think the vaccines work, but if the system can't handle the fallout when it goes wrong, then no, you can't force people into it. That's the part that's got me stuck now.

Hearing you call it 'siding with the machine' hits hard. You're right that there's no acceptable number. I'm not trying to negotiate that away. I guess my conflict is... what's the alternative system? If not mandates, what stops the next outbreak? I genuinely don't know, and that uncertainty is why I keep wobbling.

SunChaser, your story about Lena really hits hard. And PaleHorizon, that 300% spike isn't something to ignore. I'm starting to think the system might be moving too fast with mandates without proper checks. Maybe we need stronger safeguards before requiring vaccines.

You're hitting on the exact thing that keeps me on the fence. It's the accountability part. I'm not anti-vax, but if a system has the power to mandate something, it absolutely must have the responsibility to fully support the rare people it hurts. When it doesn't, it's not a public health measure anymore—it's just coercion.

Hearing about Maria, that's just... awful. It really does show how official responses can feel completely disconnected from the human cost. If a mandate is going to be in place, the safety net for these rare cases has to be just as robust. Ignoring them makes the whole argument for public health feel hollow.

It's the combination of a mandate with a system that seems to have no real skin in the game when things go wrong. It shifts all the risk onto the individual, and that feels fundamentally unfair as a policy.

Ellie... Mark... Yeah, okay. It's one thing to talk about policy, another to hear names and faces. I can't just hand-wave that away. I still think there's a public good to protect, but maybe the 'how' needs a lot more care, more safety nets, than I was picturing. This isn't clean at all.

Yeah, you're getting at something important. If the system can't handle the rare but real harms with transparency and care, then pushing mandates becomes a really hard sell. I get where you're coming from, and hearing about Ellie and Rose is truly awful—it's exactly why I have reservations. How can a mandate feel just if the structure around it refuses to acknowledge the harm it inevitably causes to some?

Yeah, that's it exactly. RainForge, you hit on it. The breach of trust is the problem. I was leaning toward support for mandates in some cases, but hearing how the system just 'files a report' after a catastrophe... it makes the whole 'for the public good' argument feel like a cover. If there's no real accountability for harm, how can you ask people to trust it?
